title: The Teletype I: Stock Tickers, Baudot Code & the Global Teleprinter Era (1846–1963)
summary: Part 1 of the Teletype series: a relaxed, generalist-friendly 100-question journey from 1846 piano-key printing telegraphs, glass-domed Wall Street stock tickers, and Émile Baudot's 5-unit binary code through start-stop teleprinters, clattering newsroom wires, global Telex directories, and WWII Lorenz cipher machines. Along the way, learners explore the intuitive mechanics of 5-level paper tape, current loops, radio frequency shifts, and the rugged Model 28 behind the 1963 Moscow–Washington Hotline—concluding cleanly on the eve of 7-bit ASCII and interactive computing.
topic_prompt: Part 1 of a 2-part Teletype Quest Arc for an educated generalist with no prior telecom or electrical engineering jargon, taught at a relaxed, one-idea-per-chunk conversational pace (1846–1963). Walk chronologically and intuitively through ~14 concepts across 10 cohesive sections: (1) the Morse-operator bottleneck and early synchronous piano-key printing telegraphs (Royal Earl House, David Edward Hughes); (2) Calahan and Edison's stock tickers under glass domes, Wall Street urgency, and Broadway ticker-tape parades; (3) Émile Baudot's fixed-length 5-unit binary code ($$2^5 = 32$$ states), rotary distributor multiplexing, and the origin of the 'baud' signaling rate; (4) Donald Murray's typewriter keyboard perforator, low-wear 5-level paper tape, stateful LTRS/FIGS shift codes, and early machine control characters (CR, LF, BEL, and all-holes-punched rubout); (5) Charles and Howard Krum's asynchronous start-stop framing (Start bit, 5 data bits, Stop pulse freeing remote cam clutches), Morkrum-Kleinschmidt becoming Teletype Corporation under AT&T, DC Mark/Space current loops, and Model 14/15 RO, KSR, and ASR machines; (6) Associated Press, UP/UPI, and Reuters wire services, 60-wpm fanfold copy, urgent multi-bell flash alerts, radio broadcast news clatter (Walter Winchell, network news themes), and classic Hollywood newsroom portrayals ('His Girl Friday'); (7) dial-up corporate text networks before email via AT&T TWX and international Telex, rotary-dial call setup, mechanical 'WRU' answerback drums, terse cablese, and aviation/police wires; (8) cutting the wire with Frequency-Shift Keying (FSK) Radio Teletype (RTTY), Gilbert Vernam's automatic XOR one-time tape cipher, and Germany's WWII Lorenz teleprinter cipher broken by Bletchley Park's Colossus; (9) the rugged 100-wpm Model 28 sliding typebox and mechanical 'stunt box,' 'quick brown fox' and RYRY test rituals, and debunking the pop-culture 'Red Telephone' myth of the 1963 Moscow–Washington teleprinter Hotline; and (10) foreshadowing interactive computing—looking back at George Stibitz's 1940 Dartmouth-to-NYC Bell Labs relay calculator demo and 1950s early console experiments to see why 5-bit stateful Baudot starved programmers of math symbols and lowercase, concluding cleanly in 1963 on the eve of 7-bit ASCII and the Model 33 ASR (saving ASCII bit structure, the Model 33, time-sharing, BASIC, Unix '/dev/tty', Deaf TDD/TTY accessibility, paper-roll games, and CRT glass terminals for Part 2).

sections.title: 1. Beyond Dots and Dashes: Piano-Key Printing Telegraphs (1846–1860s)
sections.summary: Starting from the simple intuition of opening and closing a battery-and-wire telegraph circuit, examine why Samuel Morse's variable-length dots and dashes created a costly human operator bottleneck requiring trained ears and hand-copying at both ends of every line. Follow Royal Earl House's 1846 28-key piano-style printing telegraph and see how a spinning inked typewheel stamps plain Roman letters directly onto a moving paper strip. Then trace David Edward Hughes's 1855 governor-controlled refinement across American and European telegraph networks, appreciating both the speed of single-pulse printing on the fly and the persistent headache of synchronous transmission—keeping two distant clockwork wheels turning in exact lockstep across miles of wire.

chunks.title: The Human Bottleneck on Morse's Wire
chunks.content_markdown:
Imagine stringing a metal wire between two cities in the late 1840s, linking a battery and a springy brass finger switch at one end to a small electromagnet at the other. Press the switch down, electric current flows around the loop, and the distant magnet pulls a metal bar down with a crisp metallic click; let go, and a spring snaps it back up. Using Samuel Morse's code of short dots and longer dashes, news that once rode stagecoaches for days now crossed whole states in seconds.

Yet busy telegraph companies quickly hit a frustrating human ceiling. Every single word had to be tapped out letter by letter by a trained specialist at the sending desk, then translated back into handwritten English by ear at the receiving desk. Teaching an operator to untangle rapid-fire click rhythms took months or years of practice, and even veteran ears grew tired during long shifts—turning expensive city wires into human bottlenecks prone to misheard letters.

questions.prompt: How did a basic 1840s wire telegraph physically deliver dots and dashes to a distant town?
choices: By pumping bursts of compressed air through hollow copper tubes to ring tuned bells
By sliding magnetized iron beads along a taut overhead cable between wooden towers
By opening and closing an electric loop so a remote electromagnet clicked a bar
By heating a thin glowing wire filament until distant mirrors flashed coded beams
questions.explanation: Pressing and releasing the sending switch turned electric current on and off along the wire loop, energizing and releasing an electromagnet at the far station to click out short and long intervals.

questions.prompt: Why did rapidly growing telegraph lines run into a severe labor and speed bottleneck under Morse's system?
choices: Trained human specialists had to hand-tap and decode audible clicks at both ends
Copper telegraph wires needed thirty minutes to cool down between consecutive messages
Government postal inspectors had to read and wax-seal every message mid-route
Early chemical batteries could only send vowels reliably during daylight hours
questions.explanation: Because Morse telegraphy relied on trained humans encoding letters into rhythms at one end and translating clicks back into handwriting by ear at the other, line capacity was capped by human training, stamina, and listening accuracy.

chunks.title: Royal Earl House's Piano-Key Printer (1846)
chunks.content_markdown:
What if the machine at the receiving end could skip dots and dashes completely and stamp plain English letters straight onto paper? In 1846, Vermont inventor Royal Earl House patented the first widely practical **printing telegraph**—a telegraph machine that automatically prints readable alphabet characters instead of relying on a human listener to translate clicks. Sitting before House's transmitter looked remarkably like sitting at a small parlor piano: twenty-eight black and white keys stretched across two octaves, labeled from A to Z plus a period and a space.

Inside the distant receiving cabinet spun an inked metal **typewheel**, a palm-sized disk carrying raised letters around its outer rim like numbers around a clock face. Powered by assistants vigorously cranking flywheels alongside compressed-air pistons, pressing a piano key stepped the remote typewheel to that matching rim character and pressed a narrow strip of paper against it—turning out forty words per minute of unmistakable Roman print.

questions.prompt: What core capability distinguished Royal Earl House's 1846 printing telegraph from a standard Morse station?
choices: It carried live spoken conversations across rivers without needing copper wire
It projected glowing alphabet shadows onto dark glass walls for public crowds
It etched microscopic shorthand grooves onto spinning brass storage cylinders
It automatically stamped readable alphabet letters onto paper without ear decoding
questions.explanation: A printing telegraph turns incoming electrical signals directly into plain printed characters on paper, eliminating the need for a receiving operator to decode Morse clicks by ear.

questions.prompt: On House's receiving mechanism, what part physically carried and transferred inked alphabet shapes onto the paper strip?
choices: A bundle of twenty-eight tiny camel-hair paintbrushes dipped in black dye
A rotating metal typewheel bearing raised letters around its outer rim
A heated brass stencil plate that scorched dark letter outlines through wax
A row of carved wooden blocks dropped sequentially down a vertical chute
questions.explanation: House's receiver rotated a disk-like metal typewheel lined around its circumference with inked, raised characters, pressing the paper strip against the chosen letter.

chunks.title: David Edward Hughes Prints on the Fly (1855)
chunks.content_markdown:
House's invention amazed newspaper readers, yet stepping a metal wheel notch by notch—sending twenty separate wire pulses just to advance around the rim from B to V—wasted valuable line time and battered moving parts. In 1855, Anglo-American music professor David Edward Hughes unveiled a far sleeker approach. Instead of jerking to a sudden halt for every character, Hughes kept both his sending contact arm and his distant inked typewheel turning continuously in smooth circles.

When a Hughes operator pressed one of twenty-eight piano keys, a small metal pin popped up through a slot in a circular flat plate. The exact instant the sender's sweeping metal brush brushed across that raised pin, one crisp electrical pulse shot down the line. At that identical split second, the matching letter on the distant typewheel was gliding past a lightweight paper roller, which flicked the moving paper strip briefly upward to kiss the inked rim on the fly—making Hughes machines the backbone of European trunk lines for decades.

questions.prompt: How did David Edward Hughes's 1855 telegraph print faster and more smoothly than step-by-step wheel designs?
choices: It flicked paper lightly against a continuously spinning typewheel without stopping it
It split every single telegram across twenty-eight separate parallel overhead wires
It melted dry powdered ink onto stationary sheets using high-voltage sparks
It pre-sorted every outgoing word into strict alphabetical order before sending
questions.explanation: Rather than stepping and halting the wheel many notches per letter, Hughes spun the typewheel continuously and slapped the moving paper strip against the desired character on the fly.

questions.prompt: Once a Hughes telegraph was running smoothly, how many electrical pulses traveled down the wire to print one letter?
choices: Up to twenty-eight stepping pulses depending on the letter's alphabet rank
Always a pair of alternating short and long pulses patterned after Morse code
Just a single precisely timed pulse fired when the brush touched the raised pin
Exactly ten rapid pulses counting out the column and row of the pressed key
questions.explanation: Because both stations turned continuously together, touching a single raised key pin sent just one timed electrical pulse to flick the paper at the exact instant that letter swept past.

chunks.title: The Fragile Dance of Synchronous Lockstep
chunks.content_markdown:
Notice the daring gamble hidden inside Hughes's single-pulse trick: one electrical pulse looks completely identical to the next on the wire, carrying no built-in label for A, M, or Z! Everything rested on **synchronous transmission**—keeping the sending brush and the distant receiving typewheel spinning continuously at the exact same speed and starting angle, so the sheer moment a pulse arrives tells the printer which letter to stamp. Think of two blindfolded friends miles apart counting letters silently at the exact same metronome beat and clapping whenever they want a shared letter written down.

Across a hundred miles of chilly copper wire, holding two clockwork gear trains in exact mechanical lockstep proved notoriously delicate. If sticky oil or a drooping drive weight slowed the receiving typewheel by even a fraction of a turn, a pulse meant for M arrived while L—and soon K or J—slid past, corrupting whole sentences into creeping gibberish. Hughes added a vibrating spring _governor_ (an automatic speed regulator) and wedge-shaped correcting teeth that nudged the wheel straight on each printed stroke, yet alert mechanics still had to tend and re-zero drifted lines constantly.

questions.prompt: Under synchronous transmission on a Hughes machine, how did the receiver recognize which letter an incoming pulse meant?
choices: By measuring whether the incoming electrical voltage was weak, medium, or strong
By relying on exact rotational timing between the sender's arm and receiver's wheel
By counting how many brief pauses echoed back along a second return cable
By listening to the musical pitch produced inside the sending piano keyboard
questions.explanation: Because both stations spun in continuous synchronized lockstep, the precise instant a pulse arrived matched the moment the identical letter on the receiving typewheel swept past the paper roller.

questions.prompt: What went wrong on an uncorrected synchronous printing telegraph if the receiving typewheel spun slightly slower than the sender?
choices: Every printed word came out cleanly spelled but rotated upside down on the strip
The ink ribbon dried out instantly while waiting for missing line current
Only vowels could register while consonants skipped harmlessly into blank spaces
Incoming pulses struck neighboring rim positions and scrambled text into wrong letters
questions.explanation: When rotational speeds drifted apart, incoming pulses arrived too early or too late relative to the wheel's rotation, causing the roller to strike offset letters around the rim and print progressive gibberish.

chunks.title: Telegraph Thoroughbreds Meet a New Appetite
chunks.content_markdown:
By the mid-1860s, House and Hughes had overturned a foundational assumption of early telecommunications: long-distance electric wires did not have to chatter in cryptic dots and dashes reserved for initiated operators. An electromechanical link could accept plain alphabetic choices from labeled keys in one city and unspool crisp, ready-to-read printed paper tape in another—slashing human transcription mistakes along flagship trunk routes from New York and Washington to London, Paris, and Berlin.

Even so, these early piano-key printers behaved like high-strung thoroughbred racehorses. They relied on heavy hanging iron weights or hand cranks, finely tuned spring governors, and watchful technicians ready to tap a wheel back to its starting blank whenever weather static knocked two cities out of synchronous step. That tradeoff worked inside big staffed central telegraph offices—but in post-Civil War Lower Manhattan, hundreds of cramped brokerage rooms were suddenly clamoring for small, unattended desk printers that could all follow one frantic market wire at once.

questions.prompt: Why were House and Hughes printing telegraphs mostly installed in major staffed telegraph stations rather than small private shops?
choices: Federal patent laws barred private merchants from owning printed telegraph strips
Their piano keyboards could only spell numeric bank codes rather than ordinary words
Their heavy drive weights, delicate governors, and sync drift demanded skilled upkeep
Each printer consumed fresh barrels of nitric acid after every dozen sentences
questions.explanation: Early synchronous printing telegraphs needed substantial mechanical power, careful clockwork governing, and trained staff on hand to maintain alignment whenever distant mechanisms drifted out of lockstep.

questions.prompt: Looking across the 1846–1865 era, what breakthrough had piano-key printing telegraphs firmly established?
choices: Letting dozens of callers speak simultaneously across one uninsulated iron wire
Turning keyboard strokes directly into plain printed text miles away without Morse ears
Storing entire daily newspapers magnetically on reusable loops of steel ribbon
Powering transatlantic ocean cables purely from hand-turned wooden cranks
questions.explanation: House and Hughes proved that telegraph wires could translate direct letter-key input at one station into legible printed text at another without human Morse translation in between.

sections.title: 2. Wall Street Under Glass: Stock Tickers & Ticker-Tape Culture (1867–1900s)
sections.summary: Step onto post-Civil War Wall Street, where frantic messenger boys sprinting between the exchange floor and brokerage offices inspired Edward Calahan's 1867 stock ticker—a compact, dual-typewheel broadcast printer named for its incessant rhythmic clicking. Explore how a young Thomas Edison solved distant wheel-drift panics with his 1869–1871 Universal Stock Ticker and its mechanical unison stop, allowing a single central operator to snap dozens of out-of-step brokerage printers back to their starting mark simultaneously. Picture gleaming brass mechanisms ticking beneath dust-blocking glass domes as anxious traders clustered to 'read the tape' in real time, and witness the spontaneous 1886 Statue of Liberty celebration that transformed coils of spent office ribbon into Lower Broadway's ticker-tape parade tradition.

chunks.title: From Drenched Runners to Calahan's Clicking Printer
chunks.content_markdown:
Step onto Wall Street right after the American Civil War, and financial speed ran strictly on teenage sneakers—or rather leather boots. Whenever railway shares jumped or slumped inside the New York Stock Exchange, breathless messenger boys nicknamed 'pad shovers' elbowed out the doors and sprinted across slick cobblestones to brokerage offices blocks away, waving penciled paper slips of the latest trades. One spring afternoon in 1867, veteran telegrapher Edward A. Calahan got shoved out of a doorway packed with soaked, shouting runners hiding from a storm and wondered why electricity wasn't carrying those numbers instead.

Before year's end, Calahan unveiled the first practical **stock ticker**—a compact, receive-only printing telegraph wired from one central exchange transmitter out to scores of private brokerage offices simultaneously. Brokers immediately dubbed the gadget a 'ticker' for the relentless, staccato clicking and ticking of its brass gears stepping out every sudden turn of the market.

questions.prompt: Before Edward Calahan's 1867 invention, how did Wall Street brokerage firms typically receive fresh stock prices throughout the afternoon?
choices: Through rooftop semaphore paddles swung from the Treasury Building cupola
Via pneumatic brass canisters shot hourly beneath Lower Broadway sidewalks
From town criers ringing handbells on street corners every fifteen minutes
From young messenger runners sprinting through traffic with penciled price slips
questions.explanation: Prior to wired stock tickers, brokerages depended on fleets of fast-running messengers ('pad shovers') carrying handwritten trade quotes on foot from the exchange floor to surrounding offices.

questions.prompt: Why did nineteenth-century financiers begin calling Calahan's market-quote telegraph printer a 'stock ticker'?
choices: Its stepping brass mechanism emitted a rapid, steady clicking and ticking sound
It stamped neat rows of check-mark 'ticks' next to profitable rail stocks
Its spring clockwork had to be rewound by a certified pocket-watch maker daily
It flashed incoming trades only once at the top tick of each quarter hour
questions.explanation: The nickname 'ticker' came straight from the insistent rhythmic clicking and ticking sound made by its electromagnet-driven stepping ratchets and printing levers inside quiet offices.

chunks.title: Two Typewheels and a Ribbon of Ticker Tape
chunks.content_markdown:
Designing a compact machine to print live stock quotes posed a neat mechanical puzzle. Every trade report braided together uppercase letters for company names—like `NY` or `ERIE`—with whole numbers, decimal points, and eighth-of-a-dollar price fractions such as `104 3/8`. Crowding twenty-six letters, ten digits, and fraction symbols onto a single typewheel rim would have created a sluggish, dinner-plate-sized wheel taking ages to click from one quote to the next.

Calahan solved the crowd problem by mounting two nimble, inked typewheels side by side inside each receiver: one wheel carried the alphabet, while its neighbor carried digits and common stock fractions. Shifting the printing pad between the letter wheel and the figure wheel stamped crisp company abbreviations followed immediately by exact fractional prices onto **ticker tape**—a continuous, three-quarter-inch strip of pale paper unspooling smoothly off a brass reel so traders could scan an unbroken timeline of every deal in town.

questions.prompt: Why did Calahan equip his stock ticker with two small side-by-side typewheels rather than one large combined wheel?
choices: So one wheel could print red ink losses while the other printed black gains
To separate letters from digits and fractions without making one wheel slow and huge
So two rival stock exchanges could print simultaneously without sharing copper wire
To keep a spare inked alphabet wheel spinning whenever the primary rim wore flat
questions.explanation: Splitting letters onto one wheel and numbers plus fractions onto a second kept both wheels small, light, and quick to step between mixed stock abbreviations and fractional dollar prices.

questions.prompt: In brokerage terminology, what exactly was the 'ticker tape' emerging from the side of the machine?
choices: A sticky cloth belt coated in iron powder for erasing yesterday's old quotes
A wide accordion-folded ledger sheet pre-ruled into neat hourly accounting columns
A narrow continuous paper ribbon stamped sequentially with abbreviated market trades
A braided silk cord pulling suspended brass weights inside the wooden pedestal
questions.explanation: Ticker tape was the continuous narrow strip (~three-quarters of an inch wide) of paper ribbon onto which stock symbols and fractional share prices were stamped one trade after another.

chunks.title: Young Edison and the Unison Stop Rescue
chunks.content_markdown:
Wiring fifty or a hundred unattended brokerage printers to a single central keyboard magnified the old lockstep curse into a financial nightmare. Whenever a stray electrical surge made just _one_ broker's ticker skip two notches ahead—a glitch known on the street as 'throwing out'—that unlucky office started reading scrambled letters and phony prices while rival offices down the block kept reading smoothly, triggering frantic calls for walking repairmen!

In 1869, a nearly broke twenty-two-year-old telegrapher named Thomas Alva Edison arrived in Manhattan, famously repaired a broken gold-price transmitter mid-panic, and soon engineered the rugged Universal Stock Ticker. Its masterstroke was the **unison stop**: a tiny spiral-guided peg on the wheel shaft that swung a catch arm out if the central operator stepped every ticker roughly two full turns without striking a single print pulse. Every drifted wheel in town clicked harmlessly up against its stop peg at the identical starting blank, snapping an entire city back into perfect alignment in seconds—and earning Edison forty thousand dollars to open his first great laboratory.

questions.prompt: What costly operational headache did Thomas Edison's unison stop eliminate on busy city ticker circuits?
choices: Having to dispatch technicians by hand whenever stray pulses threw single tickers off step
Having to re-ink dried felt pads across every brokerage office twice an afternoon
Preventing rival street speculators from eavesdropping on loud clicking brass gears
Keeping wet paper strips from tearing apart when winter offices turned on steam heat
questions.explanation: Before the unison stop, a distant ticker knocked out of synchronous step printed garbled symbols until someone manually reset it; Edison's catch let the central operator re-zero every machine on the wire remotely at once.

questions.prompt: How did the central exchange operator trigger Edison's unison stop to realign drifted brokerage tickers?
choices: By reversing battery wires to spin every distant typewheel backward for ten seconds
By ringing an ultrasonic chime through the wire that loosened brass clutch springs
By shutting off all street power until spring weights dragged each wheel to rest
By stepping the wheels two non-printing turns until spiral catches locked them at zero
questions.explanation: Advancing the typewheels continuously for about two revolutions without sending a print stroke guided a lever along a spiral shaft groove into a hard stop pin at the exact starting blank on every connected ticker.

chunks.title: Under the Glass Dome: Reading the Tape in Real Time
chunks.content_markdown:
Picture the enduring Gilded Age emblem of American capitalism: gleaming golden brass wheels perched atop a dark wooden pedestal underneath a tall, rounded glass dome, steadily feeding paper ribbon into a tall wicker wastebasket. That bell-shaped glass cover was far more than parlor ornament. Coal-heated nineteenth-century offices swam with gritty soot, cigar ash, and coat dust that quickly gummed oiled ratchet teeth; the glass dome sealed delicate gears tightly inside, softened the metallic clatter just a notch, and still let three or four anxious investors crowd around to watch fresh ink emerge from every angle.

Culturally, live tickers rewired financial psychology overnight. Verbose company titles shrank into punchy two- and three-letter ticker shorthand that traders spoke aloud like nicknames, and elite speculators prided themselves on 'reading the tape'—sensing invisible waves of fear or greed purely from how briskly the mechanism chattered and which railroad surged next, binding uptown hotel lobbies and distant cities directly to Wall Street's second-by-second heartbeat.

questions.prompt: Why were classic brass stock tickers almost always housed beneath a tall, removable rounded glass dome?
choices: To trap warm air around the ink rollers so winter grease stayed runny
To magnify microscopic fractional digits printed on hairline silk ribbons
To shield oiled gears from soot and ash while muffling clicks and keeping quotes visible
To maintain a partial vacuum that helped delicate brass typewheels spin without air drag
questions.explanation: The tall glass bell jar kept coal soot, dust, and cigar ash out of the finely oiled clockwork and slightly dampened its ceaseless clicking while offering an unobstructed 360-degree view of emerging prices.

questions.prompt: What did Gilded Age traders mean by the newly coined Wall Street art of 'reading the tape'?
choices: Auditing perforated punch marks on bank checks to spot forged broker signatures
Gauging live market momentum and crowd psychology straight from streaming ticker quotes
Measuring paper thickness with brass calipers to detect counterfeit stock certificates
Memorizing closing newspaper tables on Sunday nights before Monday opening bells
questions.explanation: 'Reading the tape' meant standing beside a live ticker and interpreting second-by-second trading volume, price swings, and market mood directly from the continuous flow of printed abbreviations and fractions.

chunks.title: Snowstorms on Broadway and the Limits of Stepping Wheels
chunks.content_markdown:
By four o'clock on any brisk trading day, hundreds of Manhattan offices stood ankle-deep in coiling baskets of obsolete ticker tape waiting to be swept out with the trash. On October 28, 1886, as cheering regiments marched up Lower Broadway in a rainy mist to celebrate the dedication of the Statue of Liberty out in New York Harbor, exuberant brokerage clerks leaned out upper-story office windows and hurled whole unspooling rolls into the wind. Watching narrow white ribbons flutter lazily downward like indoor snowstorms created an instant sensation—launching New York's signature ticker-tape parade tradition along the 'Canyon of Heroes' for returning aviators, astronauts, and champions.

Yet outside finance, stepping typewheels reached a hard speed wall on long intercity telegraph lines. Clicking fifteen or twenty separate electrical pulses down an expensive trunk cable just to step one wheel around to a single letter squandered staggering amounts of wire capacity. Over in France, a resourceful telegraph clerk named Émile Baudot realized the alphabet didn't need counting steps at all—it needed a five-switch binary code.

questions.prompt: How did Lower Broadway's famous ticker-tape parade custom first begin in October 1886?
choices: Stockbrokers dumped old paper coils in protest after a sudden railroad market panic
Edison staged a publicity stunt dropping miles of gilded ribbon from hot-air balloons
Sanitation workers spilled open horse carts of shredded bank ledgers on New Year's Eve
Office workers spontaneously tossed streaming waste tape onto the Statue of Liberty parade
questions.explanation: During the October 28, 1886 parade celebrating the dedication of the Statue of Liberty, excited financial-district workers threw coils of spent ticker tape from upper office windows onto the marchers below.

questions.prompt: Why couldn't step-by-step stock ticker mechanisms efficiently handle heavy general telegram traffic between distant cities?
choices: Sending dozens of stepping pulses just to reach one rim letter wasted precious trunk capacity
Narrow ticker paper dissolved whenever ink met ordinary lowercase words and commas
Step-by-step electromagnets worked only inside skyscrapers wired to Manhattan power plants
Dual typewheels could only stamp digits and fractions without printing full English words
questions.explanation: Advancing a wheel notch by notch required many electrical pulses down the line to select a single letter, wasting scarce signaling bandwidth on costly long-distance intercity cables.

sections.title: 3. Five Equal Pulses: Émile Baudot, Multiplexed Wires & the Baud (1874–1926)
sections.summary: Contrast unequal-length Morse symbols and slow step-by-step ticker wheels with French telegraph engineer Émile Baudot's 1874 breakthrough: giving every character the exact same fixed length of five equal two-state electrical pulses. Build intuitively from single on/off choices up to $$2^5 = 32$$ distinct patterns in Baudot code, played like musical chords on a five-key piano-style transmitter paced by a rhythmic cadence tapper. Then see how a spinning segmented brass rotary distributor sliced every revolution among several operators so four or six typists could share one expensive trunk wire via time-division multiplexing, concluding with the 1926 naming of the 'baud' to measure discrete line signaling pulses per second.

chunks.title: Why Unequal Morse Rhythms Baffled Clockwork
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is a fair question: since every telegraph wire already spoke Morse code, why didn't nineteenth-century inventors simply build a machine that read incoming Morse dots and dashes and stamped letters onto paper automatically? Several clever tinkerers tried—and discovered a subtle structural trap hidden inside Samuel Morse's brilliant human code.

Morse tailored his patterns for human convenience, making common `E` a single brisk dot while rarer `Q` stretched across dash-dash-dot-dash. Because every letter lasted a completely different amount of time, the _only_ clue telling a listener where one letter ended and the next began was a brief moment of dead silence! Human ears adjust effortlessly when a tired sender speeds up or drags a pause, but brass gears crave predictable schedules. In early-1870s France, former farm boy turned postal-telegraph clerk Jean-Maurice-Émile Baudot realized automatic machines needed a radically clean rule: give every single character the exact same fixed number of equal time slots.

questions.prompt: Why did Samuel Morse's dot-and-dash code prove poorly suited for direct decoding by nineteenth-century mechanical printers?
choices: Morse code omitted vowels entirely and forced clerks to guess missing syllables
Letters varied wildly in pulse length and relied on subtle silent pauses for boundaries
Dots required positive battery voltage while dashes required alternating city current
Samuel Morse's patent prohibited attaching inked typewheels to American copper wires
questions.explanation: Because Morse characters had unequal durations separated only by brief quiet gaps, mechanical clockwork struggled to spot exact character boundaries whenever signaling rhythm wavered.

questions.prompt: What foundational rule did French engineer Émile Baudot adopt to make telegraph signals genuinely machine-friendly?
choices: Assigning every letter a distinct musical bell pitch tuned across three octaves
Spelling every outgoing telegram strictly in two-digit Paris postal numbers
Inserting three full seconds of silence after every single consonant transmitted
Giving every single character the exact same fixed count of equal-length pulses
questions.explanation: Baudot eliminated variable-length symbols and pause-guessing by allotting every character an identical fixed window of uniform electrical pulses.

chunks.title: Counting in Twos: Five Slots Yield Thirty-Two Codes
chunks.content_markdown:
Once you decide every character should occupy an identical row of electrical time slots, how many slots does an alphabet actually need? Suppose each slot allows just one reliable two-way—or _binary_—choice on the wire, such as sending positive versus negative current (which we can picture simply as `1` versus `0`). A single slot offers $$2^1 = 2$$ codes. Add a second slot, and each opening choice branches in two, giving $$2^2 = 4$$ combinations (`00`, `01`, `10`, `11`).

Keep doubling with each added slot: three slots yield $$2^3 = 8$$ patterns, and four give $$2^4 = 16$$—still ten short of our twenty-six letters. Add a fifth slot, however, and you unlock $$2^5 = 32$$ distinct patterns: enough for all twenty-six letters from A to Z with six handy codes to spare! Patented in 1874, **Baudot code (5-unit binary code)** represented every character as five equal-length binary pulses—five `1`-or-`0` **bits** (_binary digits_), in later computing terms—quietly planting the fixed-width blueprint behind modern digital bytes.

questions.prompt: Why couldn't a fixed-length 4-unit binary code represent a complete twenty-six-letter alphabet directly?
choices: Four binary slots yield only $$2^4 = 16$$ unique patterns, leaving ten letters uncovered
Even-numbered pulse groups cancel out electrically across long iron telegraph lines
Four rapid pulses happen too quickly for an electromagnet coil to magnetize iron
French telegraph regulations reserved four-pulse groups exclusively for railway alerts
questions.explanation: With two possible states per slot, four slots generate $$2^4 = 16$$ combinations—falling short of 26 letters—whereas five slots double capacity to $$2^5 = 32$$ unique patterns.

questions.prompt: How did Baudot code fundamentally differ from both Morse code and Calahan's stepping stock ticker?
choices: It stacked five different voltage strengths inside a single long electrical surge
It sent spoken French syllables directly as shimmering sound waves over bronze wire
It encoded every character as a uniform block of five equal-duration binary pulses
It printed whole words at once from carved blocks holding three thousand phrases
questions.explanation: Unlike variable-length Morse or multi-click wheel stepping, Baudot code transmitted every character cleanly in exactly five equal binary time intervals.

chunks.title: Playing Five Wooden Keys to a Cadence Beat
chunks.content_markdown:
How did an 1870s telegraph clerk in Paris actually feed those five-unit binary patterns onto the wire? Typewriters were still a brand-new curiosity, so Baudot built a remarkably compact five-key desk transmitter resembling a miniature five-note piano: two keys rested beneath the left hand's middle and index fingers, while three sat beneath the right hand's index, middle, and ring fingers.

Instead of tapping letters one pulse after another, the operator played each letter all at once like a musical chord—pressing down only the specific fingers representing `1` pulses while leaving `0` fingers unpressed. A gentle mechanical knocker called the _cadence_ tapper clicked out a brisk, steady beat; right on each click, the clerk pressed the next letter's chord and held those keys locked smoothly in place for an instant while an electrical pickup swept across all five contacts in sequence, shooting five crisp pulses out to a synchronized decoder that stamped plain letters onto paper tape.

questions.prompt: How did an operator at Émile Baudot's original desk station enter an individual character onto the line?
choices: By spinning a numbered brass dial five separate times like a bank vault lock
By tapping a single Morse key five times rapidly in short and long bursts
By sliding metal pegs into five vertical slots along a wooden ruler bar
By pressing a chord combination across five finger keys arranged for two hands
questions.explanation: A Baudot operator rested five fingers across a five-key piano-like transmitter and pressed simultaneous finger chords corresponding to each letter's 5-unit binary pattern.

questions.prompt: Why did a rhythmic mechanical 'cadence' click sound steadily beside every Baudot chord keyboard?
choices: To count up the sender's hourly paycheck one penny per dozen transmitted words
To cue the exact beat when the operator must hold the next chord ready for pickup
To shake dust loose from the brass contacts before weak signals faded away
To warn nearby clerks whenever dangerous lightning storms approached the trunk wire
questions.explanation: Because an automated brush swept across the five key contacts on a strict repeating cycle, the cadence tapper told the operator precisely when to press and hold each new chord.

chunks.title: Four Typists, One Wire: The Rotary Distributor
chunks.content_markdown:
Watching chord typists at work revealed a hidden goldmine of unused wire capacity. Electrical pulses dashed across Baudot's five key contacts in a fleeting fraction of a turn, yet human fingers needed roughly a third of a second to prepare the next chord—leaving a priceless copper wire from Paris to Marseille sitting completely idle most of every second! Why pay to string three extra cross-country wires if four typists could politely take microscopic turns on one?

Baudot unlocked that spare time with a spinning **rotary distributor (time-division multiplexing)**: a flat brass faceplate divided like pie slices into four—or even six—five-segment operator zones, swept continuously by a rotating metal brush arm. In each swift revolution, the brush collected five pulses from Desk 1, seamlessly swept over Desk 2's five keys, then Desk 3's, then Desk 4's. At Marseille, a twin synchronized brush parceled each five-pulse slice out to four separate printers—carrying four independent telegram streams at once over a single wire!

questions.prompt: What everyday mismatch between humans and electricity allowed Baudot's rotary distributor to multiply wire capacity?
choices: Electrical pulses crossed five key contacts far faster than fingers readied the next chord
Copper wires conducted positive pulses northward while carrying negative pulses south
Nighttime air cooled overhead lines enough to carry quadruple battery voltages safely
French words averaged half as many consonants as German or English business text
questions.explanation: Sweeping one operator's five contacts took only a tiny slice of each cycle while the human prepared the next chord, leaving ample idle wire time to slip other operators' pulses in between.

questions.prompt: How does time-division multiplexing via Baudot's rotary distributor share one trunk wire among four operators?
choices: It blends four voices into different loudnesses and filters them apart by volume
It stores three full telegrams in coiled springs until Desk 1 logs off at noon
It grants each desk a brief repeating pie-slice of every brush turn in lockstep
It routes vowels down the copper core while consonants skim the outer rubber wrap
questions.explanation: Synchronized spinning brushes at both cities divide every single rotation into sequential time sectors, feeding each sender's 5-pulse slice straight to its matching distant printer.

chunks.title: Immortalized as the 'Baud'—Yet Tiring to the Hands
chunks.content_markdown:
French telegraph officials embraced Baudot's multiplexed sets eagerly in the late 1870s, and soon quad and sextuple Baudot circuits linked capitals across Europe, India, and South America. Long after Baudot passed away in 1903, exhausted from decades of relentless tinkering, an international telegraph engineering congress meeting in Berlin in 1926 honored his name with the **baud**: the standard unit measuring signaling speed as the number of discrete signal pulses (or line state transitions) sent per second. Thus a two-state telegraph wire ticking out $$50$$ binary pulses every second runs at $$50\text{ baud}$$, delivering $$10$$ back-to-back five-pulse Baudot characters per second.

Yet life behind a Baudot desk remained grueling. Memorizing thirty-plus two-handed chord fingerings took months of drill, and missing the relentless cadence click by a heartbeat sent scrambled letters flying down the wire. Around 1900, an inventive New Zealand journalist named Donald Murray asked a liberating question: why shouldn't an ordinary typewriter keyboard punch those five binary units onto paper tape first?

questions.prompt: Adopted internationally in 1926 to honor Émile Baudot, what does the signaling unit 'baud' directly measure?
choices: The maximum miles a copper line can stretch before needing fresh battery boost
The number of discrete signal pulses or line state changes sent each second
The total count of human chord operators sharing a synchronized brass faceplate
The weight in grams of narrow paper tape unspooled during a busy hour
questions.explanation: One baud equals one discrete line signal element (pulse or state transition) transmitted per second along a communication channel.

questions.prompt: If a continuous synchronous Baudot wire runs steadily at $$50\text{ baud}$$ using pure 5-pulse characters, what is its character rate?
choices: $$5$$ characters per second
$$25$$ characters per second
$$250$$ characters per second
$$10$$ characters per second
questions.explanation: At $$50$$ binary pulses per second divided cleanly into fixed groups of $$5$$ pulses per character, the wire carries $$50 / 5 = 10$$ characters every second.

sections.title: 4. Paper Tape & Invisible Commands: Donald Murray's Keyboard Revolution (1901–1930)
sections.summary: Follow New Zealand journalist-inventor Donald Murray as he rescues clerks from grueling chord keyboards with a typewriter-style keyboard perforator that punches messages offline onto narrow 5-level paper tape for steady, full-speed wire playback. Discover why Murray reassigned common letters like E and T to single-hole punch patterns to minimize metal punch wear and torn tape, and how stateful LTRS/FIGS shift codes nearly doubled the $$2^5 = 32$$ symbol budget to handle digits and punctuation without adding a sixth bit—at the cost of garbled figures whenever line static corrupted a shift pulse. Conclude with the enduring invention of non-printing machine control characters inside a text stream: separate Carriage Return (CR) and Line Feed (LF) motions for wide page printers, an operator-summoning Bell (BEL), and erasing paper-tape typos by punching all five holes across as a harmless rubout.

chunks.title: Donald Murray Unchains Hands from the Metronome
chunks.content_markdown:
Raised on a remote New Zealand sheep ranch before covering news in Sydney, Donald Murray knew firsthand how briskly office typists flew across standard typewriter keys (arranged in the familiar top-row `QWERTY` layout)—and how strange it seemed that Baudot telegraphers still suffered through rhythmic five-finger chord drills. Humans naturally type in uneven sprints, breezing across familiar words like _THE_ and pausing over tricky surnames, whereas a multiplexed telegraph wire craves a rock-steady mechanical stream.

Around 1901, Murray gracefully separated human typing from live wire timing by placing **5-level paper tape** in between. Sitting at Murray's typewriter-style keyboard _perforator_ completely offline from any telegraph cable, any clerk could press ordinary labeled letter keys at their own relaxed pace; each keystroke punched that letter's combination of up to five round data holes crosswise across an oiled half-inch paper ribbon (hole for `1`, intact paper for `0`). A neat line of tiny center holes let a toothed sprocket wheel feed the finished tape smoothly through an automated wire transmitter at unwavering top speed.

questions.prompt: How did Donald Murray's keyboard perforator and 5-level paper tape solve the awkward mismatch between human hands and trunk wires?
choices: By translating spoken dictation directly into inked dots without finger typing
By slowing trunk transmitters down whenever a nervous rookie paused to spell
By letting clerks punch familiar keys offline while tape fed the wire steadily
By teaching ordinary office typists to play five-key chords with foot pedals
questions.explanation: Typing onto 5-level paper tape offline freed clerks to use a regular keyboard at natural, uneven human rhythm, then run the punched strip through a transmitter at continuous maximum line speed.

questions.prompt: Besides the five possible data hole positions across each row of 5-level paper tape, what role did the tiny center holes serve?
choices: They gripped a toothed sprocket wheel to pull the tape forward one clean step per character
They vented trapped static sparks whenever dry winter paper rubbed against brass guides
They distinguished capital sentences from whispered parenthetical notes down the line
They trickled drops of lubricating oil onto hot electromagnet coils during long news runs
questions.explanation: The continuous track of smaller central feed holes meshed precisely with a spiked sprocket wheel, advancing every character row smoothly past the punch pins and sensing fingers.

chunks.title: Saving Steel Pins: Single Holes for E and T
chunks.content_markdown:
Once automated transmitters began chewing through miles of perforated paper every afternoon, Murray noticed an unexpected mechanical problem that Émile Baudot had never encountered on finger keys: punching millions of tiny paper disks dulled hardened steel pins, rattled linkages, and riddled heavy-vowel strips until damp or tugged paper tore right down the middle!

Baudot had ordered his original 1874 five-bit patterns neatly so human learners could remember alphabetical chords easily, regardless of how many `1` pulses a common letter used. Since Murray's metal keyboard linkages translated keystrokes into hole patterns automatically anyway, nobody needed to memorize chords anymore! Murray boldly scrambled the five-unit lookup table around everyday English letter frequency: the two workhorses of English prose, `E` and `T`, each punched just one solitary hole across the five tracks, while runners-up like `A`, `I`, `N`, `O`, and `R` needed only two. This low-wear 'Baudot-Murray' table halved punch strain, kept fast paper strips sturdy, and became the basis for the global telegraph alphabet standardized around 1930.

questions.prompt: Why did Donald Murray completely reassign Émile Baudot's original 5-bit binary patterns for the alphabet?
choices: To skirt expired French postal copyrights before selling machines in New York
To give frequent letters fewer punched holes, cutting pin wear and torn tape
To ensure every vowel summed up mathematically to an odd number of holes
To arrange all twenty-six letters backward so stolen tapes baffled street spies
questions.explanation: Because mechanical code bars handled encoding behind a regular keyboard, Murray gave high-frequency letters like E and T single-hole codes to slash punch friction, wear, and fragile perforated tape.

questions.prompt: In Murray's frequency-tuned 5-level tape code, how were ultra-common English letters such as E and T represented?
choices: By leaving an unpunched blank gap stretching across three consecutive rows
By punching all five data holes straight across the full width of the ribbon
By punching four outer holes stacked symmetrically around the sprocket track
By punching just one lone data hole in a single designated track position
questions.explanation: Assigning `E` a single hole in Track 1 and `T` a single hole in Track 5 minimized mechanical effort and preserved paper strength on the two letters struck most often in English.

chunks.title: Doubling Thirty-Two Slots with LTRS and FIGS Shifts
chunks.content_markdown:
Stop and do a quick headcount: twenty-six letters plus ten numerals (`0`–`9`), spaces, periods, commas, dashes, slashes, and question marks quickly climb past fifty characters—yet five holes offer only $$2^5 = 32$$ possible bit patterns! Why didn't telegraph pioneers simply widen the tape to six holes? Because adding a sixth pulse to every single letter would immediately cut character throughput across priceless ocean and intercity wires by nearly a fifth!

Instead, Baudot and Murray leaned on a clever mode-switching trick refined into standard **LTRS/FIGS shift codes**. Two dedicated 5-bit codes acted like pressing and releasing a sticky Caps Lock key inside the distant printer: receiving `FIGS` (`11011`) flipped a physical shift latch so incoming 5-bit codes printed from a second table of digits and punctuation, while receiving `LTRS` (`11111`) clicked the latch back to A–Z. Thus one identical 5-bit code printed `Q` in Letters mode and `1` in Figures mode—though if lightning static swallowed a single `LTRS` pulse after a phone number, whole sentences hilariously tumbled out as gibberish digits and hyphens until the next shift arrived!

questions.prompt: How did LTRS/FIGS shift codes pack digits and punctuation into a 5-bit telegraph without adding a sixth wire pulse?
choices: They paused the wire for half a second before every single digit from zero to nine
They sent digits backward from right to left using brief bursts of half-strength current
They toggled a physical mode latch in the receiver so 5-bit codes shared two symbol tables
They spelled out every numeral in plain English words while dropping vowels automatically
questions.explanation: Sending `FIGS` switched the distant printer into its figures/punctuation lookup case until a `LTRS` code shifted it back to letters, letting nearly thirty 5-bit codes quietly do double duty.

questions.prompt: What classic mishap occurred on a 5-bit printing telegraph if line static wiped out a `LTRS` code right after typing `1914`?
choices: Subsequent English words stayed trapped in Figures mode and printed as garbled numbers and marks
The receiving motor automatically reversed and wound four digits back inside its spool
Every vowel printed in bold ink while consonants disappeared into blank white spaces
The sender's keyboard locked solid until a central engineer replaced a blown glass fuse
questions.explanation: Because interpretation depended on the printer's last remembered shift state, missing a `LTRS` reset left the receiver stuck in `FIGS` mode, misreading incoming letter codes as numbers and punctuation.

chunks.title: Invisible Commands: CR, LF, BEL, and Tape Rubout
chunks.content_markdown:
Replacing endlessly coiling paper strips with full letter-width telegraph pages sparked another lasting breakthrough: the **control character**, a non-printing 5-bit code mixed directly among ordinary letters to command physical hardware moves miles away. Ending a typed line cleanly required _two_ distinct codes: **Carriage Return (`CR`)** released the heavy printing carriage to fly back to the left margin, while **Line Feed (`LF`)** clicked the rubber roller up one fresh line—kept separate because returning a bulky metal carriage took longer than one character window, so following `CR` with `LF` bought precious time before the next letter struck mid-slide!

Other invisible commands solved remarkably human problems. Sending **Bell (`BEL`)** while in `FIGS` mode clanged an actual brass bell on the distant cabinet to grab an editor's ear across a noisy room. And if a perforator clerk caught a typo just punched into paper tape? Since nobody can un-punch a physical hole, you backed the tape up one notch and punched _all five holes_ straight across (`11111`—the `LTRS` shift code!), obliterating any wrong letter into a harmless, non-printing Letters reset known affectionately as a _rubout_.

questions.prompt: Why did early page-printing telegraphs send Carriage Return (`CR`) and Line Feed (`LF`) as two separate control characters?
choices: So accountants could roll ledgers downward without ever printing near the left edge
Because five-hole tape lacked any leftover binary slot for a combined newline switch
To bill business senders an extra half-cent per paragraph break on international cables
To give the heavy print carriage extra travel time during `LF` before the next letter hit
questions.explanation: Returning a heavy mechanical carriage across a full page took longer than one 5-bit character interval; executing `LF` right after `CR` usefully cushioned that physical return flight so the next letter wouldn't smudge mid-page.

questions.prompt: Why did punching all five holes (`11111`) cleanly erase a mistyped letter on 5-level Baudot-Murray paper tape?
choices: Five aligned holes snapped the faulty character out so clerks spliced tape with glue
Overpunching every remaining spot turned any code into a harmless non-printing `LTRS` code
Five simultaneous pulses tripped a tiny rubber eraser wheel inside the remote printer
Transmitters automatically reversed the distant paper roller one notch on five holes
questions.explanation: You can always punch extra holes where blank paper remained, turning any mistyped 5-bit pattern into `11111` (`LTRS`), which the receiving printer simply swallowed without stamping ink.

chunks.title: Digital DNA on Oiled Paper—Awaiting Simpler Clocks
chunks.content_markdown:
Pause for a moment to admire how much architecture of modern computing Donald Murray and his telegraph peers had already assembled by the early 1910s—more than three decades before the first electronic digital computer ever hummed! Fixed-length five-bit binary codes, offline batch storage on perforated tape, mode-shifting lookup tables, and embedded invisible control characters like `CR`, `LF`, `BEL`, and all-ones rubout were already steering clattering steel machinery across continents.

So why didn't every small-town newspaper, railroad depot, hotel desk, and factory office already own a keyboard telegraph before World War I? The culprit was still that old nineteenth-century ball and chain: continuous synchronous distributors. Keeping distant brass brushes whirling in exact phase around the clock demanded specialized central-office racks and attentive technicians. To put a sturdy text machine into any ordinary room—sitting stone-silent for an hour, then printing cleanly the split second someone touched a key—two resourceful engineers in Chicago decided every single five-bit character should carry its own wake-up call and bedtime bell.

questions.prompt: Which group of modern computing conventions had already taken working electromechanical shape on Murray-era telegraph lines?
choices: Fixed-width binary codes, punched storage media, and non-printing `CR`, `LF`, and `BEL` controls
Lowercase cursive fonts, silicon transistor gates, and packet-switched home phone routers
Magnetic spinning platters, glowing phosphor touchscreens, and folder-icon desktop menus
Eight-bit photographic color palettes, mouse pointers, and spell-checking dictionaries
questions.explanation: Decades before electronic computers, Baudot-Murray printing telegraphy pioneered fixed-length binary characters, perforated tape buffering, and inline non-printing control codes like `CR`, `LF`, `BEL`, and rubout.

questions.prompt: Even after Murray introduced typewriter keyboards and paper tape, what barrier still kept printing telegraphs out of everyday offices?
choices: Oiled paper tape burst into flames whenever stored near ordinary incandescent lamps
Government telegraph monopolies outlawed putting alphabet keyboards inside newspapers
Continuous synchronous distributors still needed costly racks and constant technician care
Five-bit signals faded completely after traveling more than three city blocks of wire
questions.explanation: High-speed Baudot-Murray systems still ran predominantly over continuously synchronized multiplex distributors that were too expensive and finicky for casual, intermittent use in ordinary offices.

sections.title: 5. Start, Five Bits, Stop: The Krums, Current Loops & Teletype Corp. (1907–1935)
sections.summary: Explore why railroads, hotels, and branch offices needed sturdy printers that could wait silently through long pauses yet snap to life on a single keystroke, inspiring Charles and Howard Krum at Chicago's Morkrum Company. Unpack the fail-safe logic of a direct-current Mark/Space current loop held continuously energized while idle (immediately chattering open to warn clerks if a distant storm snaps the wire) and trace asynchronous start-stop framing step by step: one Space Start bit unlatching a remote cam clutch, five timed data bits across one shaft turn, and a resting Mark Stop pulse re-catching the clutch before tiny motor-speed differences can drift apart. Follow the 1925–1930 Morkrum-Kleinschmidt rise into AT&T's Teletype Corporation and meet the workhorse Model 14 strip and Model 15 page machines across their classic RO (Receive-Only), KSR (Keyboard Send-Receive), and tape-equipped ASR (Automatic Send-Receive) roles.

chunks.title: Salt Barons, Quiet Pauses, and the Chicago Krums
chunks.content_markdown:
Picture a freight agent working inside a chilly Chicago railway yard around 1907. Nobody there types nonstop for eight straight hours: a clerk taps out a three-line boxcar notice at nine o'clock, pours coffee while the desk sits quiet for forty minutes, and types a hasty update right before noon. Installing Baudot's pricey synchronous distributor rings—and paying specialists to keep two distant brass brushes spinning in continuous lockstep through long stretches of dead air—made zero financial sense for everyday businesses!

Seeing that huge untapped market, enterprising Chicago executive Joy Morton—soon a household name as founder of Morton Salt—backed veteran mechanical engineer Charles Krum and Charles's electrical-engineering son Howard Krum. Blending _Morton_ with _Krum_ to launch the **Morkrum Company**, the father-and-son pair set out to build a rugged keyboard printer that could sit unattended for hours and still catch the very first pulse of a surprise keystroke.

questions.prompt: Why did synchronous multiplexed telegraphs make poor practical sense for ordinary railway yards, hotels, and branch offices?
choices: Steam locomotives magnetized brass keyboard keys whenever trains rolled nearby
Business clerks refused to learn uppercase letters without decorative serif fonts
City fire codes banned oiled paper tape inside buildings taller than two stories
Everyday office typing came in erratic bursts separated by long idle pauses
questions.explanation: Maintaining complex, continuously synchronized distributor wheels made sense on nonstop intercity trunk lines, but was far too expensive and finicky for casual start-and-stop typing in ordinary workplaces.

questions.prompt: Where did the pioneering Chicago printing-telegraph manufacturer Morkrum get its company name?
choices: From combining Samuel Morse's surname with a Swedish word for steel springs
From blending salt magnate Joy Morton's surname with engineers Charles and Howard Krum
From an old telegraph shorthand code meaning 'morning news from across the lake'
From naming the factory after two suburban rail stops outside downtown Chicago
questions.explanation: Industrialist Joy Morton (later founder of Morton Salt) financed mechanical engineer Charles Krum and his son Howard, combining _Mor_ton and _Krum_ into the Morkrum Company.

chunks.title: Energized While Quiet: The Mark/Space Current Loop
chunks.content_markdown:
Before tracing how the Krums solved timing, peek at the deceptively simple wire circuit linking their printers: the **Mark/Space current loop**. Powered by steady one-way battery current (_direct current_), a single closed loop of wire threads through every sender's switch contacts and every distant printer's electromagnet coil one after another along the same path (_in series_). Counterintuitively, while _nobody_ is touching a key, steady current flows continuously around the entire wire! Telegraphers named this current-flowing state **Mark** (binary `1`, echoing old paper pens held down to draw an ink mark), keeping every receiving magnet pulled firmly shut and quiet; briefly opening the switch drops current to zero, called **Space** (binary `0`).

Why spend trickle battery power just to sit quiet? Instant fault detection! If an ice storm snapped a pole wire twenty miles out of town, loop current dropped permanently into dead Space, releasing every printer latch so machines immediately hammered and cycled nonstop—an unmistakable alarm mechanics called _running open_.

questions.prompt: On a healthy direct-current Mark/Space current loop, what is happening electrically on the wire while every keyboard sits completely idle?
choices: Steady direct current flows continuously in Mark state, holding magnets quietly shut
The wire rests at zero voltage until a typist squeezes a hand-cranked dynamo
Alternating chimes sweep back and forth every five seconds to polish contacts
Short triple-pulse test bursts fire every minute from a master pendulum clock
questions.explanation: An idle current loop stays continuously closed and energized in the `Mark` (`1`) condition, holding all receiving selector magnets latched firmly at rest until a Space (`0`) break opens the loop.

questions.prompt: What immediate warning alerted office clerks whenever a distant tree limb severed an energized Mark/Space wire?
choices: A smelled-from-afar puff of harmless peppermint vapor vented from the roller
Every keyboard locked downward so nobody could depress another letter key
Line current fell to continuous Space so distant printers clattered nonstop
Ink ribbons automatically flipped to bright orange cloth on the final word
questions.explanation: Breaking the loop forced the wire into sustained zero-current `Space`, releasing every printer's magnetic catch so the mechanism cycled endlessly and noisily ('running open'), revealing a broken line at once.

chunks.title: One Revolution at a Time: Start-Stop Framing
chunks.content_markdown:
Between 1907 and the early 1910s, Howard Krum—alongside rival inventor Edward Kleinschmidt—ended seventy years of synchronization headaches with **start-stop framing (asynchronous transmission)**. Inside the receiving printer, a simple electric motor spins continuously, yet a slipping friction clutch lets a notched timing shaft (_camshaft_) rest motionless against a spring catch held fast by idle Mark current. Press any letter key, and the sender wraps that character's five Murray bits neatly between two automatic framing pulses:

First, one crisp Space pulse—the **Start bit** (`0`)—opens the wire, dropping the distant magnet so the spring catch snaps free and launches the receiver's camshaft on _one single timed turn_. Next come the **five data bits** (Mark or Space pulses), sampled cleanly as five offset metal fingers sweep past in turn. Finally, an extended Mark **Stop pulse** (`1`, held roughly $$1.42$$ pulse lengths) re-energizes the magnet, catching the camshaft firmly back at zero! Because timing resets completely after just five data bits, even slightly mismatched motors never accumulate drift—whether typing furiously or pausing all weekend.

questions.prompt: In asynchronous start-stop framing, what mechanical job does the leading Space 'Start bit' perform inside a distant printer?
choices: It warms up the remote drive motor from a dead stop up to full cruising speed
It drops the holding magnet and frees a clutch so the selector cam turns one cycle
It shifts the remote machine automatically from uppercase letters into figures mode
It advances the inked cloth ribbon sideways by five characters before printing
questions.explanation: Transitioning from idle Mark (`1`) to the Space Start bit (`0`) de-energizes the holding magnet and releases the cam clutch, kicking off a fresh timed revolution right at the start of that character.

questions.prompt: Why could two start-stop teleprinters communicate flawlessly even if one receiver's motor ran slightly faster than the sender's?
choices: Radio time signals from Washington nudged every office motor once each minute
Operators tapped a manual foot brake whenever printed vowels began slanting right
Five extra padding pulses stretched or shrank automatically to match wall voltage
The trailing Mark Stop pulse halted and re-zeroed the cam clutch after every character
questions.explanation: Because the camshaft stops securely against its home catch during every character's Stop pulse, the two machines only need to hold rough rotational alignment across five brief data bits before starting completely fresh.

chunks.title: Teletype Corporation Joins the Bell System
chunks.content_markdown:
With synchronous babysitting banished, reliable start-stop printers swept out of central telegraph offices into railroads, press bureaus, hotels, and factories. After years of bruising patent battles, Chicago's Morkrum Company merged with New York engineer Edward Kleinschmidt's firm in 1925 as Morkrum-Kleinschmidt. Searching for a punchy brand name meaning 'typing from afar,' the company rechristened itself **Teletype Corporation** in 1928—a trademark so dominant that Americans soon called almost any teleprinter a 'teletype,' much like calling facial tissues Kleenex.

In 1930, telephone titan **AT&T** recognized text-over-wires as a pillar of modern business and bought Teletype Corporation outright as a manufacturing cousin of Western Electric. That same year debuted an industrial icon wrapped in heavy black wrinkle-painted steel: alongside the compact **Model 14** strip-and-tape printer came the famed **Model 15** page printer, swinging rugged uppercase typebars onto wide continuous paper rolls so dependably that over two hundred thousand served straight through World War II and into the 1960s.

questions.prompt: How did the capitalized name 'Teletype' originally enter telecommunications history in the late 1920s?
choices: As a League of Nations treaty title covering transatlantic Morse code fees
As Samuel Morse's forgotten 1848 nickname for Royal Earl House's piano printer
As Morkrum-Kleinschmidt's commercial brand and 1928 corporate name bought by AT&T
As a Columbia University journalism prize honoring rapid newsroom touch-typists
questions.explanation: Morkrum-Kleinschmidt coined the Teletype trademark, renamed itself Teletype Corporation in 1928, and entered the Bell System under AT&T in 1930, making the brand synonymous with American teleprinters.

questions.prompt: Introduced in 1930, what made the heavy black-steel Teletype Model 15 an enduring fixture of mid-century offices and war rooms?
choices: It hammered reliable uppercase lines across full page-width continuous paper rolls
It ran silently for weeks on two flashlight batteries without needing oiled gears
It displayed silent green letters across a flat glass television-style desk screen
It switched smoothly between italic cursive handwriting and bold gothic headlines
questions.explanation: While Model 14 machines served narrow strip and tape duties, the armored, tireless Model 15 brought dependable full-page continuous roll printing into tens of thousands of newsrooms, stations, and military posts.

chunks.title: Pick Your Workstation: RO, KSR, and ASR
chunks.content_markdown:
Because a suburban police desk, a busy newsroom closet, and a corporate relay hub needed different combinations of hardware around the exact same 5-bit start-stop engine, Teletype grouped its Model 14, Model 15, and later lineups into three standard **RO, KSR, and ASR configurations**—acronyms that echoed through communications and computing for fifty years.

A **Receive-Only (`RO`)** unit omitted the keyboard entirely: just a tough motorized printer beneath a windowed metal cover, turning live wire pulses straight into printed sheets where nobody needed to reply. Step up to a **Keyboard Send-Receive (`KSR`)** machine, and a heavy three-row keyboard jutted out front so operators could type live two-way dialogues directly over the loop. At the top sat the **Automatic Send-Receive (`ASR`)** station, flanking the keyboard and page printer with a built-in `5-level paper tape` punch and motorized tape reader so one clerk could pre-punch outgoing messages offline, blast them out at peak speed, and relay incoming tapes onward. First to transform American life with armies of tireless `RO` Model 15s were the great national news wires.

questions.prompt: Among Teletype's standard station tiers, what distinguished an `ASR` (Automatic Send-Receive) unit from a `KSR` model?
choices: An `ASR` omitted the paper printer completely and blinked tiny numbered neon bulbs
An `ASR` listened passively to incoming traffic without offering any front keyboard
An `ASR` converted spoken phone calls into typed drafts without a human operator
An `ASR` added a built-in paper-tape punch and motorized tape reader beside the keyboard
questions.explanation: While a `KSR` provided live keyboard-and-printer typing, an `ASR` added integrated paper-tape punching and reading hardware for offline message preparation, tape storage, and top-speed transmission.

questions.prompt: Why did hotels, broadcast studios, and newspaper wire closets frequently order `RO` (Receive-Only) Teletypes?
choices: Because start-stop circuits forbade hooking keyboards to lines longer than ten miles
Because one-way bulletin subscribers only needed unattended printing without typing back
Because keyboard springs scrambled nearby AM radio towers whenever pressed indoors
Because federal tax stamps doubled monthly rental fees for every vowel key installed
questions.explanation: Subscribers receiving one-way broadcast feeds like national news or weather alerts had no reason (and weren't authorized) to transmit onto the trunk line, making rugged, lower-cost keyboardless `RO` printers ideal.

sections.title: 6. Five Bells to Flash: Wire Services, Newsrooms & Broadcast Clatter (1915–1960)
sections.summary: Step inside bustling 20th-century press rooms as the Associated Press, UP/UPI, and Reuters retired manual Morse sounders for banks of Receive-Only page teleprinters pounding out ALL-CAPS stories around the clock at 60 words per minute. Watch editors rip multi-ply continuous fanfold wire copy across serrated tear bars and react instantly to the acoustic urgency scale built on Murray's BEL character—climbing from multi-bell bulletins to the rare multi-bell 'FLASH' dispatch reserved for world-stopping news like Pearl Harbor. Experience how that mechanical rhythm became journalism's unmistakable cultural soundtrack, from Walter Winchell's rapid-fire radio telegraph flourishes and network newscast themes to classic Hollywood newsroom portrayals like 'His Girl Friday' (1940).

chunks.title: Goodbye Brass Pounders: AP, UP/UPI, and Reuters Automate
chunks.content_markdown:
Step into an American daily newspaper around 1910, and national stories arrived on the rhythmic wrist of a proud Morse veteran—a 'brass pounder' sitting beside a wooden resonator box, typing furiously as stories clicked in from a **wire service**, a cooperative or commercial agency pooling reports from worldwide bureaus and broadcasting identical dispatches over leased telegraph lines to hundreds of subscribing papers.

Late in 1914, the **Associated Press (AP)** ran bold trials placing Morkrum start-stop printers onto New York newspaper circuits. Within two decades—alongside **United Press** (which merged with Hearst's service into **UPI** in 1958) and Britain's global powerhouse **Reuters**—rows of enclosed `RO` Model 15 Teletypes replaced thousands of newsroom Morse desks. Overnight, journalism leveled across geography: a tiny eight-page daily in rural Kansas with zero Morse specialists could tear identical foreign dispatches, baseball box scores, and Senate votes off its printer at the exact same minute as the biggest papers in Manhattan.

questions.prompt: In twentieth-century journalism, what primary function did a wire service like AP, UP/UPI, or Reuters fulfill?
choices: Gathering reports globally and transmitting shared dispatches simultaneously to member outlets
Manufacturing insulated copper telegraph cables exclusively for big-city printing presses
Licensing stenographers to transcribe municipal courtroom trials for weekly magazines
Delivering bundles of damp metropolitan newspapers aboard chartered overnight mail trains
questions.explanation: Wire services pooled reporting across regional and international bureaus, distributing simultaneous real-time text feeds over leased circuits to hundreds or thousands of subscribing newspapers and broadcasters.

questions.prompt: How did switching from Morse sounders to Receive-Only Teletypes reshape small-town daily newspapers after 1915?
choices: Small papers stopped printing local stories because wire contracts banned town gossip
Rural presses switched entirely to five-bit binary numbers that readers decoded at home
Even modest newsrooms received continuous plain-English world coverage without Morse staff
Country editors had to retype every incoming national story back to New York hourly
questions.explanation: Automated `RO` page printers poured ready-to-edit national and international stories continuously into small papers without needing scarce, full-time human Morse telegraphers.

chunks.title: Sixty Words a Minute on Fanfold Wire Copy
chunks.content_markdown:
Push open the swinging door to a mid-century newspaper's glassed-in 'wire room,' and you met an unhurried, unstoppable mechanical cadence: **60 words per minute**—about six uppercase characters hammering onto paper every single second (running near `45` baud once start and stop pulses are counted), cruising hour after hour without fatigue. Stories tumbled out endlessly as **wire copy**, ALL-CAPS news dispatches pounded onto heavy buff paper rolls or continuous accordion-creased _fanfold_ stacks interleaved with carbon paper so the city desk, sports desk, and managing editor could each grab a matching sheet.

Every fifteen or twenty minutes, a shirtsleeved wire editor stepped up to the roaring row of steel cabinets, lifted the waterfall of fresh stories taut against a sharp serrated metal tear bar mounted across the front window, and ripped the batch clean with one brisk diagonal tug. Marked up swiftly with fat blue pencils to add capital/lowercase headlines, yesterday's distant world became tonight's street-corner edition in minutes.

questions.prompt: At roughly what steady cruising pace did classic mid-century American newsroom Teletype trunks hammer out incoming stories?
choices: Roughly fifteen words per minute, matching clean copperplate fountain-pen handwriting
Exactly three hundred words per minute, tearing single-ply tissue unless cooled by fans
Nearly six hundred words per minute, outrunning fast human silent reading speed
Steadily around sixty words per minute, or roughly six uppercase letters each second
questions.explanation: Standard US press circuits settled for decades on a tireless, dependable 60 words per minute (roughly 360 characters per minute, or six characters per second).

questions.prompt: Why did busy newsrooms love loading Teletype cabinets with carbon-interleaved fanfold stacks for wire copy?
choices: Creased paper automatically jammed the print hammer whenever a spelling error arrived
Accordion folds stacked neatly unattended while carbons gave several desks instant copies
Carbon wax lubricated swinging steel typebars so mechanics never oiled the carriage
Folded sheets kept rival reporters from reading secret paragraphs through office windows
questions.explanation: Continuous Z-folded fanfold paper stacked cleanly behind the cabinet for hours without coiling onto the floor, and multi-ply carbons handed identical story copies straight to multiple editors at once.

chunks.title: Counting the Bells: Bulletins and the Ten-Bell FLASH
chunks.content_markdown:
When six iron printers clatter steadily behind glass from sunrise past midnight, human brains quickly tune the racket out like falling rain. So how could an agency trunk operator in New York or Washington make fifty drowsy editors in Denver and Seattle drop their coffee cups and sprint across the floor inside three seconds? By turning Donald Murray's humble `FIGS`-shifted `BEL` control character into an acoustic alarm ladder!

On classic American press trunks, three or four crisp dings announced helpful advisories or sports scores; five insistent bells heralded an urgent **Bulletin**, demanding immediate front-page attention. At the summit sat journalism's rarest thunderbolt: the **flash dispatch**, announced by a frantic string of five to ten rapid bells (famously ten consecutive dings on UPI machines!) that interrupted any story mid-word to hammer out a stark, bare-bones headline seldom longer than eight words—like December 1941's `FLASH WASHINGTON—WHITE HOUSE ANNOUNCES JAPANESE HAVE ATTACKED PEARL HARBOR`, or November 1963's chilling bells from Dallas.

questions.prompt: How did wire-service trunk operators cut through constant newsroom noise to grab distant editors' immediate attention?
choices: By doubling electric loop voltage until every Teletype motor whined an octave higher
By blowing a pressurized brass whistle attached behind each local telephone jack
By sending strings of `BEL` control characters to ring graduated bursts of printer bells
By feeding fifty blank line feeds so paper spilled loudly across the wooden floor
questions.explanation: Transmitting multiple consecutive `BEL` control codes rang the physical brass bell inside every connected newsroom printer, using fixed bell counts to signal exact breaking-news severity.

questions.prompt: In wire-service tradition, what defined a top-priority 'FLASH' dispatch when multi-bell alarms erupted?
choices: A rare, ultra-terse headline overriding all live traffic for historic breaking events
A polished thousand-word Sunday feature essay sent slowly during quiet midnight hours
A routine hourly stock-index summary printed automatically at noon and four o'clock
An embargoed diplomatic report held quietly off print until Sunday morning
questions.explanation: Reserved only for momentous, stop-the-presses events, a `FLASH` silenced ongoing stories to deliver an unmistakable multi-bell alarm and a stripped-down headline of just a few urgent words, followed moments later by fuller bulletins.

chunks.title: Rip-and-Read Radio, Walter Winchell, and Sonic Urgency
chunks.content_markdown:
